study.title: Jeremiah 20 - persecution, lamentation, and inner fire
study.overview: The chapter shows the passage of verbal persecution to physical violence against Jeremiah, the judicial response of the LORD against Pasur, and then the prophet's deeply tense prayer. Jeremiah is humiliated by proclaiming the judgment of God, but the LORD himself confirms that the message is true and that Babylon will bring captivity. Then the prophet reveals his inner conflict: he tries to shut up, but the word of God burns within him. The chapter ends with an extreme lament about his birth, exposing the emotional weight of the prophetic ministry and the raw sincerity of pain before God.

outline.title: Pasur punishes Jeremiah, and God pronounces judgment
outline.explanation: Pashur, priest and chief supervisor of the house of the LORD, hears the prophecy, harm Jeremiah and puts him in the trunk. When he was released, Jeremiah announces that the LORD himself renames Pasur as one marked by terror. The condemnation includes personal fear, death of friends, fall of Judah into the hands of Babylon, plundering the city and captivity of Pasur and his house. The text links violence against the prophet to the greater judgment that will come upon the whole nation.

outline.title: The inner struggle of the prophet and the pressure of the opponents
outline.explanation: Jeremiah now in a tone of complaint, saying that he was convinced by God for a mission that exposes him to the mockery. The message he preaches brings violence and destruction, and therefore he is ridiculed. He tries to decide not to speak in the name of the LORD, but the word becomes like fire in his bones: he cannot hold it. At the same time, he hears rumors and realizes that even friends observe his weakness waiting for his fall.

outline.title: Trust in the Lord and Delivering Cause
outline.explanation: After the outburst, Jeremiah reaffirms that the Lord is with him as a fearsome warrior. He asks the Lord to allow him to see divine vengeance, trusting that God examines the righteous and knows thoughts and feelings. The prophet then bursts into praise, declaring that God saves the soul from the needy from the hand of evildoers. Faith does not eliminate conflict, but it crosses it.

outline.title: Extreme regret: the pain of being born
outline.explanation: The chapter closes with an abrupt and radical lament. Jeremiah curses the day of his birth, the messenger who announced his birth to his father, and desires such a man to suffer ruin. He compares this misfortune to the destruction of cities over which the LORD did not come in, and imagines that it would have been better not to have gone out of the womb. The text ends without immediate relief, underlining the depth of its affliction.

study.context: By the notes provided, Pasur was a high authority priest, linked to the priestly order and responsible for maintaining the order in the temple area. Jeremiah was flogged and kept in the trunk during the night, on accusation of blaspheming against the temple. The chapter also alludes to the scene of Babylonian captivity that would come upon Judah and Jerusalem, showing that the persecution of Jeremiah is inserted in the proclamation of a greater national judgment.
study.theology: Jeremiah 20 shows the tension between faithfulness to the word of God and the human cost of that faithfulness. The prophet does not speak on his own initiative; he was called and compelled to announce a harsh message. Suffering does not mean that the message is false, but that it is offensive to those who resist God. The text also affirms the sovereignty of the LORD over judgment: he knows the righteous, sees the thoughts, and executes revenge at the right time. At the same time, the chapter preserves the honesty of the lamentation: a servant of God may be deeply slaughtered without ceasing to believe. Jeremiah's experience teaches that the life of faith can include fear, shame, desire for silence and even extreme words of pain, but the word of God continues to act as inner fire. Thus, the chapter unites judgment, vocation, perseverance and lament before God, without hiding the real weight of ministry.

scholarViews.insight: Persecution against Jeremiah advanced from words to deeds: he was flogged and put in the trunk, and then received from God a message of personal condemnation against Pasur.
Passur, who should protect Jeremiah for being a priest, becomes his persecutor; the note highlights the injustice of someone of the same priestly order to act like this.

The term translated "persuaded me" can be understood as "convincing me" or "attract me," and Clarke rejects the idea that Jeremiah is accusing God of deception; he understands that the prophet refers to the call to prophesy.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the cost of speaking the truth of God when it confronts religious and political structures?
How can we distinguish, in the spiritual life, between the faith that continues to trust in God and the sincere outburst of someone deeply wounded?
In what ways does the image of fire in the bones help to understand God's call when the human will wants to keep silent?
study.practice: Read this chapter identifying three of Jeremiah's answers: obedience, inner struggle and mourning. Then write in prayer where you have felt pressure to silence the truth, and ask God for courage to remain faithful without denying the pain. If you are suffering, imitate Jeremiah at this point: take the complaint to God before leading it to cynicism or isolation. Finally, choose a concrete practice of perseverance, how to seek spiritual support, to maintain discipline of prayer and to speak honestly without abandoning trust in the Lord.
study.uncertainty: There are important interpretative limits. The notes do not allow to define with external historical precision beyond what is said about Pasur and Babylonian captivity. Verse 7 admits tense reading: some translations suggest "persuadiste me" and others would sound like "disappoint," but the notes favor "convenced me" or "treat me" in the context of the prophetic call. There is also a difference in tone among the commentators about the final lament: some see it as a record of Jeremiah's extreme distress, not necessarily as a permanent or definitive position.
